reading.rtitle: Delayed Presentation of Cutaneous Melanoma: A Case Report
paras: INTRODUCTION. Melanoma diagnosed early is, in most cases, cured by excision alone. This case is reported not because the tumour was unusual, but because the eighteen months before presentation were.

CASE. A fifty-four year old woman presented to the dermatology clinic in March with a pigmented lesion on the left shoulder. The lesion had been present for many years, but it had changed eighteen months earlier: her daughter had noticed that the border was no longer regular. The patient had shown it to a pharmacist at the time and had been told that it was probably nothing. She did not seek further advice. While she was waiting for the appointment she had booked in January, the lesion began to bleed after a shower, and she called the clinic again.

FINDINGS AND MANAGEMENT. On examination the lesion measured nine millimetres, with asymmetry and an irregular border. A biopsy was performed at the first visit and reported five days later. The lesion was excised with clear margins under local anaesthetic. By the time she was seen, however, the tumour had metastasised to one regional node, and the disease was staged accordingly. The patient had also been lost to follow-up for eleven months at a different service two years before, which was noted in her record but had not been acted on.

DISCUSSION. Nothing in the surgery of this case was remarkable. What was remarkable was that every person the patient spoke to before March, including a healthcare professional, told her something reassuring, and none of them wrote anything down. The delay in presentation, not the tumour, is what changed the outcome.
reading.source: Teaching case written for this lesson in the format of a published case report -- the chronology and the language are the target. It is not a real patient and it must not be cited as clinical evidence.

listenings.text: Good morning. A fifty-four year old woman presented to our clinic in March with a pigmented lesion on the left shoulder. Now, the lesion itself had been there for years. What matters is that it had changed eighteen months before she came to us. Her daughter had noticed that the border was no longer regular, and the patient had shown it to a pharmacist at the time, and had been told it was probably nothing. She did not seek further advice after that. She finally booked an appointment in January, and while she was waiting for it, the lesion began to bleed after a shower, which is what made her call again. On examination it measured nine millimetres, with asymmetry and an irregular border. We biopsied at the first visit, and the lesion was excised with clear margins. By the time she was seen, however, the tumour had metastasised to one regional node. I want to be clear about why I am presenting this. The tumour was ordinary. The surgery was ordinary. The eighteen months were not, and that is the case.

I get a lot of case reports and I turn down most of them, and the reason is almost never the medicine. The commonest reason is that people think rarity is enough. It is not. Rarity is the weakest argument you can make, because a reader closes the page with nothing they can use on Monday morning. Tell me what you learned, or what you would do differently, and I will read anything. The second reason is chronology, and this one is fixable in an afternoon. Half the reports I reject have lost the order of events. Something happened, something else happened, and I genuinely cannot tell which came first, because everything is in the same tense. And if I cannot see the order, I cannot judge the decisions, and if I cannot judge the decisions there is nothing to review. And the third thing, which is really a plea. When a patient was lost to follow-up, say so, and say for how many months. Do not bury it and do not leave it out. The moment a reviewer finds a gap you tried to hide, they stop trusting the rest of the paper, and they are right to.
